title: Anthropic Broke Its $83 IPO Price. What Did Facebook Do Next?
detail:
Anthropic Broke Its $83 IPO Price. What Did Facebook Do Next?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Anthropic (ANT) closed at $82.79 on Wednesday, Nov 25. That is 0.3% below its $83 IPO price. It is also 14.8% below its $97.17 first close, only five trading days in. So what happened to other big listings that broke this fast?

On Wednesday, in Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?, we measured 10 big tech IPOs from their offer price. This piece starts the clock at the first close instead. That is the first closing price open to every buyer.

Which Big Listings Broke This Fast?

We found nine big US listings. Each fell 10% below its first close within six trading days. They are Facebook, Uber, Snap, Lyft, Airbnb, Snowflake, DoorDash, Tesla and Coinbase. Facebook, Uber, Snowflake and Lyft took one trading day. Coinbase took six.

A year after the first close, 3 of the 9 were higher. The median was 23.9% lower. All nine closed at least 33.9% below their first close within two years. The median deepest fall was 64.3%.

The last column counts trading days from the first close until the stock closed back above it, after that low. Source: Trefis, prices through Nov 25.

Only Tesla, Facebook and Uber got back above their first close within two years. Counting Lyft as the slowest, the median was 842 trading days. That is about 3.3 years.

Anthropic is already 14.8% below its first close, and all nine fell much further than that within two years. If you plan to wait for a lower price to buy, your cash does not have to sit idle while you wait. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

What Did Facebook Do Next?

It fell further, then recovered. Facebook's first close, on May 18, 2012, was $38.23. One trading day later, it was 11% lower. On Sep 4, 2012, it closed at $17.73, down 53.6%. It got back above $38.23 on Aug 5, 2013, 303 trading days after listing. Two years after its first close, it was up 58.3%.

Lyft is the other ending. Its first close, on Mar 29, 2019, was $78.29. Less than a year later, in the March 2020 crash, it closed at $16.05. That was 79.5% down. It has never closed above $78.29 again.

Is It The Market?

Not since the listing. From Anthropic's first close on Nov 19 to Wednesday's close, the S&P 500 fund (SPY) rose 0.1%. It went from $715.87 to $716.70. Anthropic fell 14.8% over the same days. Tuesday, Nov 24, was a bad day for chip stocks. The chip fund (SMH) fell 7.3%, Nvidia fell 5.9% and Anthropic fell 6.5%. But the slide since the first close is Anthropic's own.

Could It Be A Buy Now?

For three of the nine, the record says yes. Airbnb, Snowflake and Tesla were higher a year after the first close, by 17.7% to 27.4%. Facebook lost a third in its first year. But it was 58.3% above its first close after two years. Google listed in August 2004. It never closed 10% below its first close in its first two years. It was up 179.1% after one year.

In our view, the calendar made the biggest difference. Six of the nine listed from 2019 to 2021. Then they met the March 2020 crash or the 2022 bear market. Nine cases is a small record, and the market's path drove much of it. Anthropic is also far bigger than any of them was at its first close. It was valued at about $1.11 trillion at Wednesday's close.

What If Anthropic Follows Their Paths?

Apply each of the nine deepest falls to Anthropic's $97.17 first close. Tesla's shallowest fall, 33.9%, would mean $64.23 a share. That is 22.4% below Wednesday's close.

In dollars, $100,000 put in at the Nov 19 first close of $97.17 was worth $85,200 at Wednesday's close. On the median path, it would fall as low as $35,700. A year in, it would be worth $76,100. On Tesla's path, the low would be $66,100. On Coinbase's, it would be $9,900.

Every one of the nine fell at least a third within two years. So in our view, a close near $64 at some point before November 2028 should not surprise anyone.

Two things could change that picture. The first is Anthropic's first quarterly report as a public company. It would matter if it showed sales above the $68 billion yearly pace of its September quarter. That is the growth case in our piece Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? The second is Dec 15, the next step in the lock-up. A lock-up bars early holders from selling for a time. Up to 303 million shares come free that day. Getting past it without a new low would matter too.

What Can A Long-Run Investor Do?

In our view, hold a position you can live with under either ending. Size it so the median fall hurts without doing real damage to the whole. At 1% to 3% of a portfolio, a 64.3% drop costs 0.6% to 1.9% of the whole.

One plan is to set buying prices in advance, before the next headline. For example: a third at a price you would pay today, a third at $64 and a third at $35. That avoids buying because it broke the IPO price, or selling because it did.

Facebook holders who sized for the fall and set their prices owned a stock up 58.3% two years on. Lyft holders who did the same lost a small, planned amount. The record does not pick the ending. It can help you decide how much to own.

No one knows which ending Anthropic will get. That is why, in our view, it is safer to own many strong companies than to rely on one.

Ives dismissed concerns around the market being heavily reliant on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, terming it a "gilded age", and noting that several executives are irreplaceable.

His comments came after he raised his price target on Nvidia to $250 from $225 on Tuesday, to reflect the value of Huang's return.

Futurum Equities analyst Shay Boloor on Wednesday noted that the amount of market value that Nvidia has lost and gained over the past few trading sessions is equal to the entire market capitalization of smaller companies such as Costco, Starbucks, Airbnb, or Pfizer.

Yorkville Ives senior managing director, Dan Ives, on Wednesday stated that Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's value extends far beyond the chipmaker itself, while calling the recent turbulence in the market around Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO and subsequent reinstatement as part of a wider "growth scare" in the AI cycle.

"Jensen is worth a trillion dollars to the valuation of Nvidia, and I'd argue probably $8 trillion to $10 trillion to the overall market value of what we see, not just in AI, but to the real market," Ives said in an interview with Bloomberg, while adding that the recent market turbulence does not imply a break in the AI growth cycle.

"There's a growth scare. There's worries about what's happening relative to financing and data center buildout. It's been a perfect storm."
– Dan Ives, Partner and Senior Managing Director, Yorkville Ives & Co.

Ives also dismissed concerns of the market being heavily reliant on Huang, terming it a "gilded age", and noting that several executives are irreplaceable, such as Meta Platforms (META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Palantir Technologies's (PLTR) Alex Karp, and Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella.

'Gut Check Moment' For AI Trade

Demand remains strong for Nvidia products, Ives noted. Even if China and several other Asian markets were removed from the equation, he argued demand-to-supply ratios for Nvidia chips would remain roughly 10-to-1.

"If you ordered a chip today in the U.S. for Nvidia, you can't get that chip till end of 2028," Ives said. He added that a large share of planned data centers, including the ones in Texas, are already permitted, dismissing concerns of a data center slowdown after the democratic takeover in the U.S. midterm elections.

The current pullback in tech stocks represents a "gut check moment" rather than the end of the AI trade, he added.

title: Airbnb vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Airbnb vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 8:35 AM PST 7 min read
ABNB
UBER
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The rise of the gig economy has produced two dominant platforms that changed how people travel and commute. Deciding between Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) and Uber Technologies (NYSE:UBER) requires looking at their different paths to growth.

Airbnb operates a high-margin marketplace for lodging and experiences, while Uber Technologies focuses on high-frequency mobility and delivery services. Both companies have moved past their early loss-making stages to become profitable enterprises. This comparison examines their business models, financial health, and current valuations to determine which stock is better positioned for investors through 2027.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a massive global marketplace for stays and unique experiences, supporting more than 9 million active listings across 220 countries and regions. The company maintains a specialized Co-Host Network that pairs property owners with support personnel and utilizes Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) for its critical cloud infrastructure. This strategy contributes to the growth of consumer discretionary stocks within the global travel market.

During the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, the company reported that revenue reached about $13.9 billion, representing a growth rate of roughly 16.7% compared to the previous year. Net income for this period was around $3.2 billion, reflecting a consistent demand for travel across major markets like the United States and the United Kingdom. This financial performance shows the ability of the platform to generate significant profits while expanding into newer geographic territories.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio is roughly 1.4x, which compares current assets to current liabilities to show how easily the company can cover short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $4.6 billion, though note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 34% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Uber Technologies

Uber Technologies connects riders, drivers, and merchants through a platform that spans mobility, delivery, and freight across more than 15,000 cities. The company has established major partnerships with retailers like Best Buy (NYSE:BBY) and Tractor Supply Company (NASDAQ:TSCO) to provide on-demand delivery services to their customers. It also maintains a strategic relationship with Amazon, allowing Prime members to access fee-free orders through its delivery app.

Key Takeaways

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the third quarter, nine bought Airbnb, including Cathie Wood's ARK Invest, and 12 sold, including Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments.

The sellers moved far more money, but two of the three biggest still own large Airbnb stakes, and Fisher sold only 1,600 shares.

Five of the buyers also sold or cut Palo Alto Networks, and the biggest buyer sold Booking Holdings and trimmed Expedia.

The buyers look right: at 27x forward earnings, near its five-year low, Airbnb can reach the Street's $206 target if today's estimates hold.

Big funds couldn't agree on Airbnb (ABNB:NASDAQ) last quarter.

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30 (funds investors know by name, or ones with $1 billion or more of US stocks in their 13Fs, leaving out quant and index funds), nine bought Airbnb. Each opened a position or added 20% or more to one. Twelve sold out or cut their stakes by 20% or more, and 28 held the stock at the quarter's end. Since Sept. 30, Airbnb is up 6%.

The buyers kept their bets small

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest added 48% to its stake, taking it to 218,989 shares, its 13F filed Nov. 13 shows. That's about $11 million of buying. The whole stake was worth $35 million at Sept. 30, just 0.2% of its 13F stocks for a firm that manages $17 billion. The biggest buyer was Meridiem Capital Partners, a $2.4 billion fund, which opened a 262,877-share position worth about $42 million, 1.8% of its 13F stocks. KR Capital, a $1.2 billion fund, raised its stake 169% to 91,405 shares. Larry Robbins' Glenview Capital and Lee Ainslie's Maverick Capital each opened stakes of about $2 million.

The sellers moved far more money

Independent Franchise Partners, a $24 billion fund, cut its stake 20%, a sale worth about $178 million at quarter-end prices. That one cut is more than twice what all nine buyers added together. Yet it still held 4.32 million shares worth $693 million at Sept. 30, 4.3% of its 13F stocks. Consulta, a $3.1 billion fund (that's what its 13F holds in US stocks), cut its stake 29%. Airbnb is still its fifth-largest holding, at 7.8% of its 13F stocks.

The clean exit came from Akre Capital, a $12 billion fund, which sold all 1.18 million of its shares, about $169 million worth. Airbnb had been 3.3% of its 13F stocks a quarter earlier. Tom Gayner's Markel cut its stake 70%. And Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments, which manages $387 billion, sold all 1,600 of its shares. That's about $229,000, a rounding error for a firm that size.

title: Airbnb vs. DoorDash: Which Stock Is a Better Buy?
detail:
Airbnb vs. DoorDash: Which Stock Is a Better Buy?
Jack Delaney, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 11:45 AM PST 5 min read
ABNB
DASH
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors often weigh growth potential against current profitability when comparing Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) and DoorDash (NASDAQ:DASH). Both companies have transformed how consumers spend on experiences and daily conveniences, but their financial trajectories remain distinct.

Airbnb focuses on the global travel market by connecting hosts with guests seeking unique accommodations. DoorDash operates a local commerce platform that facilitates delivery from restaurants and retail merchants. While both benefit from digital shifts, their cost structures and capital requirements differ significantly.

Image source: Getty Images.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a two-sided global marketplace that connects more than 5 million hosts with guests across roughly 220 countries. The company focuses on expanding its brand through strategic partnerships with cultural and entertainment organizations to attract a diverse range of travelers. This positioning within consumer discretionary stocks allows it to capture spending on both short-term vacations and long-term stays.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $13.9 billion, representing growth of approximately 16.7% over the prior year. The company demonstrated significant bottom-line strength by generating a net income of close to $3.2 billion during this same period. This level of profitability is a hallmark of its asset-light business model, which avoids the costs of owning physical properties.

The case for DoorDash

DoorDash operates a local commerce platform that connects merchants, consumers, and delivery couriers across more than 40 countries. The company has evolved beyond restaurant delivery into grocery and convenience sectors, maintaining agreements with over 600,000 merchants. Growth is further supported by over 56 million monthly active users and a proposed $17 billion acquisition of Instacart to solidify its market position.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $17.1 billion, which is a significant 35% increase compared to the previous twelve-month period. The company also reached a milestone by reporting a net income of approximately $1.1 billion.

Risk profile comparison

Airbnb faces intense competition from established online travel agencies like Booking Holdings (NASDAQ:BKNG) and Expedia Group (NASDAQ:EXPE), as well as traditional hotel chains. The company is also subject to evolving legal and regulatory environments, particularly restrictive short-term rental laws in major markets like New York City. Additionally, reliance on third-party payment processors and other threats present ongoing operational risks.

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) has historically posted strong growth metrics. This is usually what happens when businesses disrupt massive industries and quickly steal market share.

Momentum is picking up. During the third quarter (ended Sept. 30), the company reported a year-over-year revenue gain of 19%, beating analyst estimates. Gross booking value climbed 21%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Besides the growth story, investors shouldn't overlook Airbnb's impressive profitability. Trailing-12-month free cash flow (FCF) of $4.9 billion accounted for 35% of revenue, which is a superb margin. The board of directors had the confidence to approve a $12 billion buyback, in addition to the $2.7 billion in existing capacity.

The growth stock has had a wonderful year. It's up 33% in 2026 (as of Nov. 18). Here's what that share repurchase runway means for investors.

Image source: Getty Images.

A shrinking share count benefits long-term owners

Airbnb is known for having sizable stock-based compensation, totaling $1.4 billion over the last nine months. This is how businesses, particularly those earlier in their life cycles, pay their employees. But it results in an increase in the share count.

To Airbnb's credit, though, its outstanding share count shrank by almost 3% in the past year. The company conducted $4 billion in stock buybacks over the last 12 months. Combining the new $12 billion repurchase authorization with the $2.7 billion remaining capacity means Airbnb now intends to buy 12% of the company's entire market capitalization.

Investors benefit from this tailwind. A smaller outstanding share count provides a jolt to earnings per share (EPS). Shareholders who continue to hold the stock see their ownership percentage in the business increase over time.

The best companies can balance returning capital to investors with reinvesting into their operations. Airbnb is certainly still playing offense.

The business continues to expand its list of services. Travelers can now book hotels. And there are more active partnerships in place. And for hosts, a redesigned calendar makes juggling multiple listings far simpler.

Airbnb is also leaning into the opportunity that artificial intelligence (AI) presents. It plans to release an AI-powered travel assistant in 2027.

Airbnb has delivered a strong 49.1% share price gain over the past year, even as headlines range from AI travel tools to new hotel partnerships and regulatory questions around its use of Chinese AI models. With the stock recently closing at US$170.36, the live question for investors is whether that price can be supported by the cash Airbnb is expected to generate over time.

The 49.1% return over the past 12 months puts real weight on whether Airbnb's current share price lines up with what its future cash flows can reasonably justify.

Moves into hotels and an AI travel agent may support expectations for higher booking volumes and more efficient operations, which directly affect how much cash the business can produce and when it arrives.

For investors, the debate is whether Airbnb's recent share price level is adequately backed by the intrinsic value indicated by its cash flows under the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) approach.

If you want a second reference point while you assess Airbnb's cash flows, a focused screen of 40 high quality undervalued stocks.

Is Airbnb Still Cheap on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model looks at the cash Airbnb can return to shareholders over time and adjusts it back to today's dollars. On this view, the business is being valued on the strength of a last twelve month free cash flow figure of about $5.0b, with analysts expecting that annual cash generation to continue growing toward roughly $9.1b by 2030.

The projections assume Airbnb keeps converting its platform into larger free cash flow over the next decade, rather than stalling out at current levels. This helps explain why the estimated intrinsic value comes out substantially above the current share price of $170.36. The push into hotel inventory and a full-service AI travel agent points to management leaning into these expectations for higher long term cash generation. At the same time, growing scrutiny of its use of Chinese AI models underlines why the market may still be cautious on how much future cash to price in today. "They've launched long-term rentals, made over 500 product improvements, and are going all-in on AI to make the platform smoother..."

Airbnb (ABNB) stock returned 53.2% over the past twelve months, against 11.0% for the S&P 500. After that rise, the question is what could lift the shares next. What is that business, and how far along is Airbnb with it?

Airbnb Now Lists Thousands Of Hotels

The business is hotels. The platform now lists thousands of boutique and independent hotels across more than 60 top destinations. During the November 5 call, management said hotel bookings accelerated again in the third quarter of fiscal 2026. Hotels are also growing markedly faster than Airbnb's core business.

It is still early, though. Hotels are growing "off of a very, very tiny base," in management's words. Management said the hotel industry has also come round to Airbnb, after some animosity in the early 2010s. In its view, hotels now see it as a major ally, because it brings them an audience that is disproportionately Gen Z.

How Big Could Hotels Get For Airbnb?

Management called hotels a $900 billion market. It said Airbnb will make multiple billions of dollars in hotel revenue in the coming years.

To view that against the whole company, Airbnb recorded revenue of $13.9 billion over the twelve months to September 30, 2026. That was up 16.7%, following growth of 10.2% in the twelve months before. A few billion dollars from hotels would be a large addition to Airbnb, not a sideline.

Airbnb stock trades at 7.6 times sales, against 3.1 for the S&P 500. On November 18, the shares closed 5.4% below their highest close of the past year. Buyers at that price appear to assume the company keeps growing well ahead of the market, and hotels offer one place that growth could come from.

What Does Airbnb Still Have To Prove?

Airbnb still has to give a forecast for hotels. On the November 5 call, management declined to give any projection for the hotel business. Until it does, you cannot measure how much hotels add.

New businesses also cost money, and that shows in how much of each booking Airbnb keeps. The share of bookings Airbnb kept as revenue was 17.6% in the third quarter, down slightly from a year earlier. Management said that was mainly due to Reserve Now, Pay Later, which lets guests book now and pay closer to the stay. A smaller part came from incentives and credits for new business initiatives.
